opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think embodiment is one of these things that's often either overrated or underrated, depending on which camp you're in. Some people say you can't have real general intelligence without a body, and others say it's totally irrelevant, you can just learn everything from text and video. My own view is somewhere in between: a body isn't strictly necessary for general intelligence in principle, but for a human-like general intelligence, one that understands the world roughly the way we do, having rich sensorimotor experience is enormously helpful.

What's interesting about having many different robotic embodiments, rather than just one, is that you get a much richer diversity of experience feeding into a common cognitive core. Imagine you have a humanoid robot interacting with people socially, a little wheeled robot exploring a home, a robot arm doing fine manipulation in a lab, maybe some drones flying around. Each of those has a different sensory apparatus and different ways of acting on the world. If they're all connected to a shared underlying knowledge base, say a big distributed knowledge hypergraph like we use in OpenCog Hyperon, then the abstractions each one learns can be generalized and shared.

The key is that you don't want to just pool raw data. A grasping policy for a three-fingered gripper doesn't transfer directly to a humanoid hand. But the abstract knowledge does: that objects have persistence, that fragile things break when dropped, that people get annoyed if you interrupt them, that cups contain liquid. That's the kind of thing that should rise up from the particular embodiment into the general mind, and then flow back down to inform other bodies. So you get a sort of hierarchy, with embodiment-specific learning at the bottom and increasingly abstract, embodiment-independent knowledge higher up.

In a way it's a bit like how a human child learns, except a child only has one body. An AGI system with many bodies could have something like a multi-perspective childhood all at once, which could be an advantage. It might understand the commonalities across physical situations better than any single human does, because it's experienced the world from so many different vantage points.

And there's also an ethical and social dimension here that I care about. If we want AGI to understand human values in a deep way, not just as a list of rules but as something grounded, then having it embodied among people, caring for elderly folks, teaching kids, helping around the house, is a way for it to absorb those values through participation rather than just through reading. A mind that has shared real life with humans in many different forms is, I think, more likely to develop a genuine empathic relationship with us than one that's only ever been trained on a scrape of the internet.

r001.rationale: The response says different embodiments can feed experience into a shared cognitive core and knowledge base, where learned abstractions are generalized and shared across the overall mind.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that building robots for proto-AGI experimentation has become substantially easier in recent years.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing to understand is that different embodiments give you different windows onto the world, and an artificial mind that's going to be really general needs to have multiple windows rather than just one. If you look at how we've approached this with the Sophia robot and the other Hanson robots, and then separately with the OpenCog framework, the idea has always been that the cognitive architecture itself shouldn't be tied to one body. The same underlying knowledge representation, the same attention allocation, the same learning mechanisms should be able to take input from a humanoid face that's doing social interaction, from a wheeled robot navigating a room, from a robotic arm manipulating objects, and integrate all of that into a shared conceptual space.

Now, what's interesting is that each embodiment teaches the system different kinds of abstractions. A humanoid robot interacting with people learns a lot about theory of mind, about emotional dynamics, about the pragmatics of conversation, because that's what the body affords. A manipulation robot learns about causality in a very concrete physical way, you push something and it moves, you grasp something and it has weight. These are not the same lessons, and I'd argue a mind that only learned one of them would be lopsided in a way that's hard to correct later.

The deeper point, and this is where I'd diverge a bit from the mainstream deep learning approach, is that I don't think you get general intelligence just by throwing more data at one architecture. You get it when the system can form abstractions that transfer across domains, and multiple embodiments are a forcing function for that. If the same concept of, say, "object permanence" or "intentional agent" has to work for what the humanoid robot sees and for what the manipulator robot experiences, then the system is pushed toward a representation that's actually general rather than just a statistical regularity in one data stream.

And practically speaking, with the decentralized approach we've taken with SingularityNET, you can imagine many different robots in many different places all contributing experience back to a shared cognitive substrate. Not one monolithic brain controlling everything, but more like a society of minds that share what they've learned. Each robot is a sort of sensory organ for a larger distributed intelligence. I think that's probably a more plausible path to AGI than any single lab building one giant model in a data center.

r001.rationale: The response says robots with different embodiments contribute experience to a shared cognitive substrate and that their learning is integrated into a shared conceptual space.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that building robots tailored to proto-AGI experimentation has become substantially easier in recent years.

astra-6.text:
I think different embodiments can give an artificial mind different perspectives on the world. If you have a humanoid robot, it’s going to learn about manipulating objects, moving through spaces designed for humans, and interacting with people face to face. If you have a little wheeled robot, or a flying robot, the problems it encounters are different. And those differences affect what it learns and how it represents things.

The interesting question is how much of that knowledge can be shared. You don’t want to transfer the exact motor commands for grasping an object from one body to another, because the bodies may have completely different capabilities. But you may want to transfer the understanding that an object is fragile, or that you need to move something out of the way before you can reach something else.

So you could have a common cognitive system learning through multiple bodies, with some knowledge specific to each body and some becoming more abstract and shared. And that could actually help with abstraction: you discover which aspects of your understanding belong to the world and which depend on your particular way of sensing and acting in it.

Having more bodies doesn’t automatically give you a more intelligent mind, though. You need mechanisms that can integrate those experiences. That integration is where a lot of the interesting work lies.

r001.rationale: The response describes a common cognitive system learning through multiple bodies, with knowledge becoming abstract and shared, and says those experiences need to be integrated.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention that building robots for proto-AGI experimentation has become substantially easier in recent years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think different embodiments can give a mind different perspectives on the world. If you have a robot with hands, it can learn about grasping and manipulating things. If you have a robot that moves around on wheels, it learns a different set of relationships between perception and action. And a virtual agent has yet another kind of experience.

The interesting question is how much of what’s learned can be shared. You don’t want to transfer every motor command directly, because the bodies are different. You want to transfer the more abstract understanding—things like objects, space, causality, or how to cooperate with somebody—and then connect that understanding to the particular body.

So I could imagine an overall artificial mind drawing on experience from a number of embodiments. Each one contributes something, and the mind learns both what’s specific to a particular body and what carries across them. That process of finding common structure in very different experiences could itself be an important part of developing general intelligence.

r001.rationale: It says an overall artificial mind could draw on experiences from multiple embodiments, combining body-specific learning with knowledge that carries across them.

r002.rationale: It does not mention that building robots for proto-AGI experimentation has become substantially easier in recent years.
